newsitem.title: UK: Oil prices set new high on resumed Kurdish fighting.
newsitem.headline: Oil prices set new high on resumed Kurdish fighting.

text.p: World oil markets jumped back in the saddle and rode higher again on Monday, shrugging off last week's heavy price fall amid renewed concerns over winter heating oil supplies and tensions in the Middle East.
London November futures for bellwether North Sea Brent crude set a new post-Gulf War high of $24.92 a barrel before easing to close at $24.80, still 82 cents up on the day.

Rival Kurdish factions in northern Iraqi Kurdistan resumed hostilities over the weekend, reminding oil traders of the missing crude supplies previously expected under the U.N.'s postponed oil-for-food exchange with Iraq.

"Iraqi oil exports under U.N. resolution 986 this year are now impossibly remote, and in the light of recent developments in the Kurdish areas of Iraq, they may well not begin until the second half of 1997 -- if at all," said the Centre for Global Energy Studies (CGES) in London.

The U.N. deal, signed in May, was suspended at the end of August after Baghdad sent troops to intervene on behalf of the Kurdistan Democratic Party (KDP) against its rival, the Patriotic Union of Kurdistan (PUK).
U.N. officials said on Monday that the anti-Baghdad PUK had regained control of part of the territory lost, including the region's largest city, Sulaimaniya.
The KDP accused Iran of sending troops and arms to lead PUK attacks over the weekend, but Tehran denied any involvement.
"The threat of a domino effect in the oil-rich Middle East is a real worry to oil traders," said Peter Gignoux, head of the energy desk at brokerage Smith Barney.
Analysts said the renewed fighting underlined how difficult it would be for the United Nations to guarantee the safety of aid distribution monitors in northern Iraq any time soon.
Meanwhile Western oil markets are still suffering a chronic shortage of winter heating oil and diesel supplies.

With U.S. heating oil stocks too low for comfort, a refinery fire in Toledo, Ohio, led to a rally in U.S. heating oil futures and served to remind the market of its vulnerability to any supply shorftall.
Oil fell sharply on Friday as traders took profits from prices at five-and-a-half year highs.
Buyers stepped back in for heating oil on Monday as forecasts emerged for colder than normal weather in the U.S. northeast, the world's biggest heating oil market.
"With oil sales from Iraq almost certainly out of the question...the oil market looks set to remain tight through the coming winter -- whatever the weather," said the CGES.
The oil cartel OPEC looks unlikely to respond to strong demand for its crude by raising its output ceiling when it meets again at the end of November.

OPEC, including linchpin member Saudi Arabia, has no plans to raise output for fear of rocking the boat and undermining a market which is providing windfall extra revenues, Middle East Gulf sources said last week.

"If Iraqi oil is unlikely to materialise and Saudi Arabia, along with its Gulf allies, is reluctant to open the taps because of subsequent revenue losses, only a mild winter is capable of taking the heat out of the oil market," said the CGES.
